triples.relationship: same-book renewed prophetic commission
triples.rationale: The opening verse introduces the Lord's word to Jonah. Chapter 3 explicitly says that the word came to him a second time, marking the renewal of this commission after his flight and rescue.
triples.source_text: The word of the Lord came to Jonah, the son of Amittai, saying:

target_units.text: The word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying:

triples.relationship: city's wickedness brought before God
triples.rationale: The Lord sends Jonah to Nineveh because its wickedness has come up before Him. Genesis similarly presents Sodom and Gomorrah's increasing cry and great sins as coming before the Lord ahead of intervention concerning the cities.
triples.source_text: “Rise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim in it, for the outcry of its wickedness has come up to Me.”

target_units.text: And the Lord said, “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has increased, and their sins are exceedingly great.
So I will go down and see whether they are being brought to an end according to their cry which comes to Me; and if not, that I may know.”

triples.relationship: flight from God's presence and the sea
triples.rationale: Jonah boards a ship in an attempt to flee from the Lord's presence. The psalm asks where anyone could flee from God's face and says that even at the sea's farthest reaches His hand remains present.
triples.source_text: But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord. He went down to Joppa, found a ship traveling to Tarshish, paid its fare and boarded it, to sail with them to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.

target_units.text: Where can I go from Thy Spirit, and where can I flee from Thy face?
If I ascend to heaven, Thou art there; if I descend into Hades, Thou art present.
if I take up my wings at dawn and settle at the sea’s farthest reaches,
indeed, even there Thy hand will guide me, and Thy right hand will hold me fast.

triples.relationship: the Lord raises a storm at sea
triples.rationale: Jonah's ship is endangered when the Lord stirs up a wind and a great surge arises at sea. The psalm's account of seafarers likewise attributes a storm wind and rising waves to the Lord's command.
triples.source_text: The Lord stirred up a wind upon the sea, and there was a great surge on the sea; the ship was in danger of being shattered.

target_units.text: Those going down into the sea in ships, doing work on many waters,
they saw the Lord’s works and His wonders in the depth.
He spoke, and a storm wind stood, and its waves were raised.

triples.relationship: narrative parallel of a sleeper in a storm
triples.rationale: Jonah sleeps below while the sailors fear for their storm-tossed ship. Mark likewise places a sleeping central figure in a boat endangered by a great storm. The comparison concerns the narrative situation; Jonah's flight and Jesus' later command have different roles in their respective stories.
triples.source_text: The sailors were afraid, and each was crying out to their god. They threw the equipment in the ship into the sea, to lighten their load. But Jonah had gone down into the hollow of the ship, and was sleeping and snoring.

target_units.text: A great windstorm arose, and the waves broke into the boat, so that the boat was already filling.
He was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. They woke Him and said to Him, “Teacher, dost Thou not care that we are perishing?”

triples.relationship: parallel emergency unloading at sea
triples.rationale: Jonah's sailors throw equipment into the sea to lighten the ship during the storm. Acts describes storm-battered sailors throwing cargo and then the ship's tackle overboard.
triples.source_text: The sailors were afraid, and each was crying out to their god. They threw the equipment in the ship into the sea, to lighten their load. But Jonah had gone down into the hollow of the ship, and was sleeping and snoring.

target_units.text: As we were violently battered by the storm, the next day they began throwing cargo overboard.
On the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands.

triples.relationship: narrative parallel of awakening the sleeper
triples.rationale: The officer calls Jonah to rise from sleep and pray so that those aboard will not perish. Mark's disciples likewise awaken Jesus with a question about their perishing, connecting the awakening with the boat's danger.
triples.source_text: The ship’s officer approached him and said, “Why are you snoring? Rise and call upon your god, so that the god may bring us safely through and we may not perish.”

target_units.text: He was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. They woke Him and said to Him, “Teacher, dost Thou not care that we are perishing?”

triples.relationship: parallel identification of an offender
triples.rationale: The sailors use lots and Jonah is identified as the cause of their trouble. Joshua narrates the successive indication of Judah, a clan and finally Achar in the investigation of Israel's offense. The shared pattern is identification of a particular offender within a larger afflicted group; Joshua's supplied wording says indicated.
triples.source_text: Each said to his neighbor, “Come, let us cast lots and learn on whose account this calamity is among us.” They cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.

target_units.text: Joshua rose early and brought the people forward by tribes. The tribe of Judah was indicated.
They were brought forward by clans, and the Zerahite clan was indicated. They were brought forward man by man,
and Achar son of Zambri, son of Zerah, was indicated.

triples.relationship: parallel questioning after identification
triples.rationale: After Jonah is identified, the sailors demand an account of the cause of their calamity and his background. Joshua similarly questions the identified Achar, demanding disclosure of what he has done, and receives a confession.
triples.source_text: They said to him, “Tell us on whose account this calamity is among us. What is your occupation? Where do you come from? What country and what people are you from?”

target_units.text: Joshua said to Achar, “Give glory today to the Lord, the God of Israel, and make confession. Tell me what you have done, and do not hide it from me.”
Achar answered Joshua, “Truly I have sinned before the Lord, the God of Israel. This is what I did:

triples.relationship: shared confession of the Lord as creator
triples.rationale: Jonah identifies the God he reveres as the Lord of heaven who made the sea and dry land. Exodus likewise describes the Lord as maker of heaven, earth and sea, explaining the scope of the deity Jonah names while at sea.
triples.source_text: He said to them, “I am a servant of the Lord, and I worship the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”

target_units.text: For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the seventh day and made it holy.

triples.relationship: same-chapter progression of the sailors' fear
triples.rationale: The sailors fear greatly and already know of Jonah's flight from the Lord because he had told them. After the sea is calmed, verse 16 again describes their great fear, now explicitly directed to the Lord and expressed in sacrifice and vows.
triples.source_text: The men were greatly afraid and said to him, “What is this you have done?” For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.

target_units.text: The men feared the Lord with great fear, offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows.

triples.relationship: same-chapter proposed remedy and narrated outcome
triples.rationale: Jonah says that throwing him into the sea will make it cease raging against the sailors. Verse 15 narrates that action and the sea's resulting cessation, completing the proposal with its stated outcome.
triples.source_text: Jonah said to them, “Lift me up and throw me into the sea; then the sea will subside for you. For I know that this great surge is upon you because of me.”

target_units.text: They took Jonah and threw him out into the sea, and the sea stopped its tossing.

triples.relationship: parallel struggle against hostile waters
triples.rationale: The men strain to return Jonah's ship to land but cannot overcome the sea. Mark describes disciples straining at the rowing because the wind is against them, a corresponding scene of difficult human effort on hostile waters.
triples.source_text: But the men strained to return to land and could not, for the sea kept rising more fiercely against them.

target_units.text: When evening came, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and He was alone on the land.
Seeing them straining at the rowing, for the wind was against them, He came toward them about the fourth watch of the night, walking on the sea. He intended to pass by them.

triples.relationship: shared prayer against innocent-blood guilt
triples.rationale: The sailors ask the Lord not to lay innocent blood upon them as they prepare to throw Jonah overboard. Deuteronomy provides a communal plea that innocent-blood guilt not remain among the people; both prayers explicitly seek release from that bloodguilt.
triples.source_text: They cried out to the Lord and said, “By no means, Lord! May we not perish for this man’s life, and do not lay innocent blood upon us, for Thou, Lord, hast done as Thou didst wish.”

target_units.text: Be merciful unto Thy people Israel, whom Thou hast redeemed, O Lord, out of the land of Egypt, that there be no guilt of innocent blood among Thy people Israel. And atonement shall be made for the blood on their behalf.
And you shall remove the guilt of innocent blood from among yourselves, if you do that which is good and pleasing before the Lord your God.

triples.relationship: prayer followed by the storm's cessation
triples.rationale: The sea ceases after the sailors' prayer and their action toward Jonah. The psalm likewise narrates seafarers crying to the Lord and the storm being commanded to settle, with the waves falling silent.
triples.source_text: They took Jonah and threw him out into the sea, and the sea stopped its tossing.

target_units.text: They cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and He brought them out of their distresses,
and commanded the storm, and it settled into a breeze, and its waves fell silent.

triples.relationship: narrative parallel of sudden calm
triples.rationale: Jonah's narrative moves from a raging sea to its cessation when he is thrown overboard. Mark narrates wind ceasing and a great calm after Jesus' command; both episodes emphasize the abrupt end of a dangerous storm, while specifying different actions preceding it.
triples.source_text: They took Jonah and threw him out into the sea, and the sea stopped its tossing.

target_units.text: And He awoke, rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Be silent; be still.” And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.

triples.relationship: sacrifice and vows in response to deliverance
triples.rationale: The sailors offer sacrifice and vows to the Lord after the sea calms. The psalmist likewise promises burnt offerings and payment of vows declared in affliction, joining distress, deliverance and worship.
triples.source_text: The men feared the Lord with great fear, offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows.

target_units.text: I will enter Thy house with whole burnt offerings; I will pay Thee my vows,
which my lips declared and my mouth spoke in my affliction.

triples.relationship: fear following the calming of the sea
triples.rationale: Jonah's sailors greatly fear the Lord after the storm ends. Mark's disciples are greatly afraid after Jesus calms the wind and sea and ask who He is, connecting the resulting fear with power over the waters.
triples.source_text: The men feared the Lord with great fear, offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows.

target_units.text: They were greatly afraid and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?”

triples.relationship: explicit later comparison to Jonah
triples.rationale: Jonah is in the sea creature's belly for three days and three nights. Jesus explicitly cites Jonah's confinement for that duration when comparing it with the Son of Man being in the heart of the earth.
triples.source_text: The Lord commanded a great sea creature to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the sea creature’s belly three days and three nights.

target_units.text: He answered them, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, but no sign will be given it except the sign of Jonah the prophet.
For just as Jonah was in the sea creature’s belly three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights.

triples.relationship: prayer from mortal danger
triples.rationale: Jonah prays to the Lord from the sea creature's belly. The psalm describes the dangers of Hades and then a cry for the Lord to rescue the speaker's soul, corresponding to prayer from the peril described by Jonah's surrounding narrative and prayer.
triples.source_text: Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the sea creature’s belly,

target_units.text: The pangs of death surrounded me; the dangers of Hades found me; I found affliction and pain.
And I called on the name of the Lord: “O Lord, rescue my soul!”

triples.relationship: shared prayer language of affliction and Hades
triples.rationale: Jonah recalls crying in affliction and being heard from the belly of Hades. The psalm likewise joins Hades, affliction, crying to God and God's hearing of the voice from His holy temple.
triples.source_text: and said: “In my affliction I cried to the Lord my God, and He listened to me. From the belly of Hades Thou didst hear the voice of my cry.

target_units.text: The birth pangs of Hades surrounded me; the traps of death overtook me.
And when I was afflicted, I called upon the Lord and cried out to my God. He heard my voice from His holy temple, and my cry before Him will enter His ears.

triples.relationship: shared billows-and-waves prayer language
triples.rationale: Jonah says that all God's billows and waves passed over him in the sea's depth. The psalm uses the same combination of God's billows and waves passing over the speaker in its language of the deep.
triples.source_text: Thou didst cast me into the depths of the heart of the sea, and rivers encircled me. All Thy billows and Thy waves passed over me.

target_units.text: Deep calls upon deep at the sound of Thy waterfalls; all Thy billows and Thy waves passed over me.

triples.relationship: shared lament of exclusion from God's sight
triples.rationale: Jonah says he has been thrust away from God's eyes and asks about looking again toward the holy sanctuary. The psalm similarly recalls the alarmed claim of being cast away from God's eyes, followed by acknowledgment that God heard the petition.
triples.source_text: I said, ‘I have been thrust away from Thine eyes. Shall I again look toward Thy holy sanctuary?’

target_units.text: But I said in my alarm, “So I have been cast away from before Thine eyes.” For this reason Thou heardest the voice of my petition when I cried unto Thee.

triples.relationship: shared imagery of overwhelming waters
triples.rationale: Jonah describes water poured around him as far as his life and the surrounding abyss. The psalm cries for rescue because waters have reached the soul and the speaker has entered the sea's depths, sharing the imagery of life overwhelmed by water.
triples.source_text: Water poured around me up to my life; the uttermost abyss encircled me; my head sank into clefts of mountains.

target_units.text: Save me, God, for waters have entered as far as my soul.
I was stuck in the mud of the depth, with no firm ground; I entered the sea’s depths, and a tempest drowned me.

triples.relationship: descent toward death and appeal for rising
triples.rationale: Jonah describes descent into a land with eternal bars and asks that the ruin of his life rise up. The psalm credits the Lord with bringing the soul up from Hades and saving it from those descending into a pit. The connection is descent toward death and divine rescue; Jonah's supplied petition is preserved as a petition.
triples.source_text: I descended into a land whose bars are everlasting restraints; and let the ruin of my life rise up, Lord my God.

target_units.text: Lord, Thou broughtest my soul up from Hades; Thou didst save me from those descending into a pit.

triples.relationship: prayer reaching God's holy temple
triples.rationale: Jonah remembers the Lord as his life fails and says his prayer may come into the holy sanctuary. The psalm describes an afflicted cry heard by God from His holy temple, connecting distress with prayer reaching God's dwelling.
triples.source_text: As my life was failing me, I remembered the Lord; may my prayer come to Thee, into Thy holy sanctuary.

target_units.text: And when I was afflicted, I called upon the Lord and cried out to my God. He heard my voice from His holy temple, and my cry before Him will enter His ears.

triples.relationship: remembering God when the soul is troubled
triples.rationale: Jonah remembers the Lord when his life is failing. The psalm likewise connects the soul's trouble with remembering God, giving a close parallel to the prayer's movement from distress to remembrance.
triples.source_text: As my life was failing me, I remembered the Lord; may my prayer come to Thee, into Thy holy sanctuary.

target_units.text: My soul was troubled within me; therefore I will remember Thee from the land of Jordan and Hermoniim, from a small mountain.

triples.relationship: shared rejection of empty vanities
triples.rationale: Jonah says that those guarding vain and false things abandoned their mercy. The psalm also speaks of those guarding vanities to no purpose and contrasts that practice with hope in the Lord.
triples.source_text: Those who guard vain and false things abandoned their mercy.

target_units.text: Thou didst hate those who guard vanities to no purpose; but I hoped in the Lord.

triples.relationship: sacrifice of praise and payment of vows
triples.rationale: Jonah promises sacrifice with praise and thanksgiving and payment of his vows. The psalm explicitly commands a sacrifice of praise and payment of vows, followed by the promise of rescue when God is called upon in affliction.
triples.source_text: But I, with a voice of praise and thanksgiving, will sacrifice to Thee. Whatever I vowed I will repay to Thee, for deliverance to the Lord!”

target_units.text: Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God and pay your vows to the Most High.
Call on Me in the day of affliction; I will rescue you, and you will glorify Me.” Diapsalma.

triples.relationship: deliverance belongs to the Lord
triples.rationale: Jonah closes his promise of worship with deliverance directed to the Lord. The psalm directly declares that salvation belongs to the Lord, matching the prayer's attribution of rescue to Him.
triples.source_text: But I, with a voice of praise and thanksgiving, will sacrifice to Thee. Whatever I vowed I will repay to Thee, for deliverance to the Lord!”

target_units.text: Salvation belongs to the Lord, and Thy blessing is upon Thy people.

triples.relationship: same-chapter commands framing confinement
triples.rationale: The Lord first commands the sea creature to swallow Jonah. Later the creature is commanded, and it casts him onto dry land; the later command's content is unstated. The two reported commands frame his confinement and release.
triples.source_text: The sea creature was commanded, and it cast Jonah out onto dry land.

target_units.text: The Lord commanded a great sea creature to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the sea creature’s belly three days and three nights.

triples.relationship: same-book renewed prophetic commission
triples.rationale: The Lord's word comes to Jonah a second time here. The opening verse records the first coming of that word, so the repeated introduction explicitly marks the renewed commission.
triples.source_text: The word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying:

target_units.text: The word of the Lord came to Jonah, the son of Amittai, saying:

triples.relationship: same-book renewed commission to Nineveh
triples.rationale: The renewed command sends Jonah to Nineveh and expressly refers to the former proclamation. The opening command names the same city and charges him to proclaim there because its wickedness has come before God.
triples.source_text: “Rise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim in it according to the former proclamation that I spoke to you.”

target_units.text: “Rise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim in it, for the outcry of its wickedness has come up to Me.”

triples.relationship: same-book reversal from flight to obedience
triples.rationale: Jonah now rises and goes to Nineveh according to the Lord's word. Earlier he rose to flee to Tarshish from the Lord's presence; the two departures contrast resistance with obedience to the commission.
triples.source_text: Jonah rose and went to Nineveh as the Lord had spoken. Now Nineveh was a city great before God, about a three-day journey.

target_units.text: But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord. He went down to Joppa, found a ship traveling to Tarshish, paid its fare and boarded it, to sail with them to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.

triples.relationship: explicit later reference to Jonah's proclamation
triples.rationale: Jonah's recorded proclamation warns that Nineveh will be overthrown in three more days in this source edition. Matthew explicitly refers to the Ninevites repenting at Jonah's proclamation, identifying the preaching whose effect the narrative records.
triples.source_text: And Jonah began to enter the city, about a day’s journey, and he proclaimed and said, “Three more days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”

target_units.text: Men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at Jonah’s proclamation; and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.

triples.relationship: explicit later reference to Nineveh's repentance
triples.rationale: Nineveh's people believe God and proclaim a fast with sackcloth. Matthew explicitly describes the men of Nineveh as having repented at Jonah's proclamation and makes their response a witness at the judgment.
triples.source_text: The people of Nineveh believed God, proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from their greatest to their least.

target_units.text: Men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at Jonah’s proclamation; and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.

triples.relationship: fasting joined to turning toward God
triples.rationale: Nineveh's people respond to the divine warning with belief, fasting and sackcloth. Joel calls for turning to the Lord with fasting and wholehearted repentance, connecting the outward fast with the response to God.
triples.source_text: The people of Nineveh believed God, proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from their greatest to their least.

target_units.text: “And now,” says the Lord your God, “turn to Me with your whole heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning.”
Tear your hearts, not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, because He is merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy, and relents concerning calamities.

triples.relationship: parallel royal humbling after a prophetic warning
triples.rationale: Nineveh's king leaves his throne and royal clothing and puts on sackcloth upon hearing the message. Ahab likewise responds to the prophetic word by weeping, tearing his tunic, wearing sackcloth and fasting, after which the Lord acknowledges his humbling.
triples.source_text: The word reached the king of Nineveh. He rose from his throne, took his robe off himself, wrapped himself in sackcloth and sat in ashes.

target_units.text: Because of the word, Ahab was stricken before the Lord: he went about weeping, tore his tunic, tied sackcloth around his body, fasted, and put on sackcloth on the day he struck Naboth the Jezreelite.
The Lord’s word came through His servant Elijah concerning Ahab, and the Lord said,
“Have you seen how Ahab has been stricken before Me? I will not bring the harm in his days, but in his son’s days I will bring the harm.”

triples.relationship: parallel communal abstention from food and drink
triples.rationale: Nineveh's royal decree forbids food and water for the people and livestock. Esther similarly commands the gathered Jews in Susa to fast without eating or drinking. The shared feature is a publicly directed fast with both food and drink withheld; Nineveh's decree additionally includes livestock.
triples.source_text: It was proclaimed and declared in Nineveh from the king and his nobles: “Let people and livestock, cattle and sheep, taste nothing; let them not graze or drink water.”

target_units.text: “Go, assemble the Jews in Susa, and all of you fast for me. Neither eat nor drink for three days, night and day; I and my maids will also go without food. Then I will enter the king’s presence contrary to the law, even if I must perish.”

triples.relationship: fasting accompanied by rejection of injustice
triples.rationale: Nineveh's response joins sackcloth and crying to God with each person turning from evil and the injustice in their hands. Isaiah likewise says that sackcloth and outward fasting are inadequate and calls instead for releasing people from injustice and caring for the vulnerable.
triples.source_text: People and livestock clothed themselves in sackcloth, and they cried earnestly to God. Each turned away from his evil way and from the injustice in their hands, saying:

target_units.text: I did not choose this fast, or a day for a person to humble his life. Even if you bend your neck like a ring and spread sackcloth and ashes beneath you, you will not thereby call it an acceptable fast.

‘It is not such a fast that I chose,’ says the Lord. ‘Instead, loosen every bond of injustice, undo the strangling ties of coercive agreements, release the crushed, and tear up every unjust written contract.
Break your bread for the hungry and bring homeless poor people into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him; do not overlook those belonging to your own family.

triples.relationship: shared hope that God may relent
triples.rationale: Nineveh's people ask who knows whether God will relent and turn from wrath so they do not perish. Joel likewise asks who knows whether He will turn and relent, expressing hope rather than assuming the outcome.
triples.source_text: “Who knows whether God will relent and turn from His fierce anger, so that we certainly do not perish?”

target_units.text: Who knows whether He will turn and relent and leave a blessing behind Him, a sacrifice and drink offering for the Lord our God?

triples.relationship: narrative example of conditional judgment
triples.rationale: God sees Nineveh turn from evil and does not bring the announced calamity. Jeremiah explicitly states that when a threatened nation turns from its evils, the Lord will change His mind concerning the destruction He planned.
triples.source_text: God saw their deeds, that they had turned from their evil ways. God relented concerning the calamity He had said He would bring upon them, and He did not do it.

target_units.text: At last I will speak concerning a nation or kingdom, to remove them and destroy,
and if that nation turns from all their evils, I will change My mind concerning the evils I planned to do to them.

triples.relationship: narrative analogy of resentment at mercy
triples.rationale: Jonah is grieved after Nineveh is spared, and his following prayer names God's mercy as the issue. The older son likewise objects when his father welcomes the returning son, and the father explains why restoration calls for joy. The relationship is a shared response of resentment at mercy extended to another.
triples.source_text: Jonah was grieved with great grief and was disturbed.

target_units.text: But he became angry and was unwilling to enter. His father came out and pleaded with him.
But he answered his father, ‘Behold, all these years I have served you as a slave, and I never disobeyed your command; yet you never gave me a young goat so that I might be glad with my friends.
But when this son of yours came, who devoured your livelihood with prostitutes, you slaughtered the fattened calf for him!’
And he said to him, ‘Child, you are always with me, and everything of mine is yours.
But we had to be glad and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and came to life; he was lost and was found.’”

triples.relationship: shared declaration of God's merciful character
triples.rationale: Jonah describes God as merciful, compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy when explaining his flight. Exodus's proclamation of the Lord's name uses the same cluster of merciful attributes.
triples.source_text: He prayed to the Lord and said, “O Lord, were these not my words while I was still in my own land? That is why I was quick to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that Thou art merciful and compassionate, patient, abundant in mercy, and relenting concerning calamities.

target_units.text: The Lord passed before him and proclaimed, “The Lord God, compassionate and merciful, slow to anger, abundant in mercy and true,

preserving righteousness and showing mercy to thousands, taking away lawlessness, injustice, and sins, yet not cleansing the guilty, bringing the fathers’ lawlessness upon children and children’s children to the third and fourth generation.”

triples.relationship: shared mercy and relenting formula
triples.rationale: Jonah explains that he knew God was merciful, compassionate, patient, abundant in mercy and one who relents concerning calamities. Joel uses that same sequence of attributes to ground the appeal to turn to the Lord.
triples.source_text: He prayed to the Lord and said, “O Lord, were these not my words while I was still in my own land? That is why I was quick to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that Thou art merciful and compassionate, patient, abundant in mercy, and relenting concerning calamities.

target_units.text: Tear your hearts, not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, because He is merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy, and relents concerning calamities.

triples.relationship: parallel prophet's request for death
triples.rationale: Jonah asks the Lord to take his life because death seems better to him. Elijah likewise asks the Lord to take his life during his distressed withdrawal, giving a close parallel between the two prophets' death wishes.
triples.source_text: And now, Master Lord, take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.”

target_units.text: He himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness, came, and sat under a single broom bush. He asked that his life might end and said, “Let it be enough now! I pray Thee, take my life from me, Lord, for I am no better than my fathers.”

triples.relationship: same-chapter repeated question about grief
triples.rationale: The Lord first asks whether Jonah is deeply grieved after Nineveh is spared. The question recurs with the gourd named explicitly in verse 9, drawing Jonah's reaction to the city and his reaction to the plant into comparison.
triples.source_text: The Lord said to Jonah, “Are you deeply grieved?”

target_units.text: God said to Jonah, “Are you deeply grieved about the gourd?” He said, “I am deeply grieved, even to death.”

triples.relationship: divine shelter from the sun
triples.rationale: God provides the gourd to shade Jonah's head and shelter him. The psalm describes the Lord as a shelter and promises that the sun will not scorch the one He guards, corresponding to the protection the plant gives before its removal.
triples.source_text: The Lord God commanded a gourd, and it grew up above Jonah’s head, to provide shade over his head and shelter him from his troubles. Jonah rejoiced over the gourd with great joy.

target_units.text: The Lord will guard you; the Lord is your shelter at your right hand.
By day the sun will not scorch you, nor the moon by night.

triples.relationship: same-book motif of commanded creatures
triples.rationale: God commands a worm that strikes Jonah's protective gourd. Earlier He commanded the sea creature to swallow Jonah. Both episodes show a creature changing the prophet's circumstances under divine command, within the book's larger contrast with Jonah's initial flight from his own command.
triples.source_text: God commanded a worm at dawn the next day; it struck the gourd, and it dried up.

target_units.text: The Lord commanded a great sea creature to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the sea creature’s belly three days and three nights.

triples.relationship: same-book motif of divinely sent winds
triples.rationale: God commands a scorching wind on land, and the text then reports the sun striking Jonah's head. Earlier the Lord stirred up a wind at sea, explicitly followed by a great surge. Both episodes feature divinely directed winds, while describing their accompanying events differently.
triples.source_text: As the sun rose, God commanded a burning, scorching wind. The sun struck Jonah’s head; he lost heart, renounced his life and said, “It is better for me to die than to live.”

target_units.text: The Lord stirred up a wind upon the sea, and there was a great surge on the sea; the ship was in danger of being shattered.

triples.relationship: same-chapter repeated question about grief
triples.rationale: The Lord asks about Jonah's deep grief over the gourd, repeating the earlier question after the city's deliverance. The repetition prepares the comparison between the plant Jonah values and Nineveh's people and livestock.
triples.source_text: God said to Jonah, “Are you deeply grieved about the gourd?” He said, “I am deeply grieved, even to death.”

target_units.text: The Lord said to Jonah, “Are you deeply grieved?”

triples.relationship: same-chapter lesser-to-greater compassion argument
triples.rationale: The Lord points to Jonah sparing a brief-lived gourd for which he had not labored. The next question applies that concern to the far greater case of Nineveh with its many people and livestock, completing the argument about compassion.
triples.source_text: The Lord said, “You spared the gourd, over which you did not toil and which you did not nurture, which came to be in a night and perished in a night.

target_units.text: And shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which dwell more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know their right from their left, and much livestock?”

triples.relationship: divine compassion extending across God's works
triples.rationale: The Lord's question includes both Nineveh's numerous people and its livestock in the reason for sparing the city. The psalm describes the Lord as merciful and His compassions as extending over all His works, corresponding to the breadth of that concern.
triples.source_text: And shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which dwell more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know their right from their left, and much livestock?”

target_units.text: Compassionate and merciful is the Lord, patient and abundant in mercy.
The Lord is kind to all, and His compassions are over all His works.

triples.relationship: parallel divine questions about sparing a people
triples.rationale: The Lord asks whether He should not spare Nineveh. Hosea similarly presents God's questions about how to deal with Ephraim and His refusal to act according to furious anger or erase them. The populations differ, but both speeches make divine compassion central to withholding destruction.
triples.source_text: And shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which dwell more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know their right from their left, and much livestock?”

target_units.text: How shall I deal with you, Ephraim? Shall I shield you, Israel? How shall I deal with you? Shall I make you like Adama and like Seboim? My heart turned within itself; My change of mind was stirred together.
I will certainly not act according to My furious anger; I will certainly not abandon Ephraim to be erased. For I am God and not a human being, holy within you, and I will not enter a city.
